desc: Many species of bears roam the wilderness. Most would rather be left alone, but make for fearsome foes when provoked.
Dogs can be found on farmsteads and city streets trailing close behind their masters, ever ready to fight at their sides.
The wilds of Skyrim teem with deer and rabbits - docile creatures that commonly serve as prey for the province's more savage beasts.
Goats and cows are a common sight in Skyrim's farming settlements. The Nords depend on the meat, milk, and hides of these animals to keep their bellies full and the cold at bay.
The frigid waters of the north are inhabited by horkers - large creatures that can be easily outrun and are widely hunted for their tusks and meat.
Navigating the rugged northern landscape is easier astride a horse, available for purchase from the stables in any of Skyrim's major settlements.
The horses of Skyrim may be slower than those from Cyrodiil, but what they lack in swiftness is made up for in hardiness.
Mudcrabs lurk along the banks of lakes, rivers, and the northern coast. They can easily be mistaken for rocks while motionless, and use this natural disguise to ambush their prey.
Nix-hounds are insectoid pack hunters that use their long proboscises to drain their prey of blood, leaving behind only an empty husk.
Skeevers are large rodents that make their nests in caves and sewers. Although easy to kill, they pose a challenge in groups and carry debilitating diseases.
Many of Skyrim's waterways are home to slaughterfish, whose razor-sharp teeth have claimed the lives of many careless swimmers.
Frostbite spiders rank among Skyrim's most despised creatures. Attacking indiscriminately with fangs and toxic venom, they are as deadly as the affliction for which they are named.
Travelers should beware of Skyrim's wolves, even on the roads. They are feral beasts that hunt in packs to take down any prey available - whether it walks on four legs or two.
Each of Skyrim's nine holds features a capital city with its own jarl, laws, and culture. Of these, five are considered major cities: Riften, Solitude, Markarth, Whiterun, and Windhelm.
Skyrim's settlements are patrolled by guards, whose duty is to respond to crime and defend their hold's inhabitants. Respect the law to avoid confrontation.
Guards may sometimes be persuaded to overlook petty crimes. Those with titles of prestige may find lawkeepers to be more lenient.
Each hold handles crime independently. A criminal wanted in Whiterun might have no bounty in Solitude, and so on.
The Nords first conquered Markarth from the native people of the Reach thousands of years ago. In 4E 174, a group of Reachmen briefly seized the city during an event known as the Markarth Incident.
Riften sits on the eastern shore of Lake Honrich, partly built over its waters. The canal that spans the city was once a major thoroughfare for merchants and fishermen.
Beneath the city of Riften lies a network of sewer tunnels known as the Ratway - a hideout for various lowlifes and the base of operations for the notorious Thieves Guild.
Riverwood is a logging town on the White River that has thrived since the Merethic Era, resting beneath the shadow of Bleak Falls Barrow to its west.
Skyrim's capital, Solitude, is the heart of Imperial power in the province. The city was built atop a natural arch, lending its port much-needed shelter from the winds of the Sea of Ghosts.
The stone-walled Castle Dour is the oldest structure in Solitude. It acts as the Imperial army's base of command, while the jarl resides in the Blue Palace.
Whiterun's central location in Skyrim has made it a major trading hub. The city comprises three districts, with the towering fortress of Dragonsreach dominating the highest.
No one is certain who built the Skyforge, where the Companions' weapons are made. Its discovery led to the construction of Jorrvaskr and the Companions as they are recognized today.
Windhelm is a former capital of Skyrim and the oldest human city on the continent. Built as a monument to mankind, it has withstood multiple sackings in its long history.
The Jarl of Windhelm resides in the Palace of Kings, seated upon the ancient throne of Ysgramor like many legendary figures before him.
Skyrim is embroiled in a bloody civil war between the forces of the Third Empire, mobilized in the west, and the Stormcloak rebels of its east.
The Stormcloaks view the banning of Talos worship as an affront to Nord culture, while the Imperials believe Skyrim must honor the laws of the Empire that Tiber Septim himself built.
Soldiers from both sides of the civil war are known to establish camps in enemy-controlled regions, offering shelter and provisions for their faction's troops.
War camps are usually well-manned, but lack the proper defenses of a castle. Raiding enemy encampments is an effective tactic for weakening their positions.
The Imperial Legion is the military force of the Empire, locked in conflict with the Stormcloaks. Led by General Tullius, they fight to restore control over Skyrim.
The Empire claimed victory in the Great War, but narrowly - at the cost of Hammerfell and much of its former might. The Legion now fights to quell the rebellion and keep Skyrim within the fold.
General Tullius is the Military Governor of Skyrim tasked with crushing the Stormcloak Rebellion, viewing its leader as nothing more than a power-hungry usurper.
"May those above judge me, and those below take me, if I fail in my duty. Long live the Emperor! Long live the Empire!" - Part of the Imperial Oath
Serving under the authority of the Emperor, the Imperial Legion - with its vast numbers and strict discipline - is regarded as one of the most powerful fighting forces ever assembled.
Many soldiers of the Imperial Legion oppose the ban on Talos worship, yet still believe the Empire offers the best chance for victory against the Thalmor.
The old Nord phrase "season unending" casts war as an endless cycle, where combatants pause only to gather strength before the next battle.
The Stormcloaks are rising up against Imperial rule to reclaim religious and political freedom in Skyrim. They view Ulfric Stormcloak as the true High King and a paragon of Nordic values.

High King Torygg was recently killed by Ulfric Stormcloak, who shouted him apart with the power of the Thu'um. Ulfric was thereafter branded a traitor by the Empire, and the Stormcloak Rebellion began in earnest.
"Throw off the shackles of Imperial oppression. Do not bow to the yoke of a false emperor. Be true to your blood, to your homeland." - Anonymous, Nords Arise!
While their ranks are not limited to Nords, the Stormcloaks assert that they alone are the true sons and daughters of Skyrim.
Ulfric Stormcloak is the rebellious Jarl of Windhelm, a veteran of the Great War who harbors deep resentment for the White-Gold Concordat and its ban on Talos worship.
No one agrees whether the Empire branded them "Stormcloaks" as an insult, or if Ulfric coined the name himself. Regardless, the rebels wear it like armor in their fight for a free Skyrim.
Despite being raised by necromancers, a bone wolf can become a loyal companion, rewarding friendship by carrying items and boosting the effectiveness of attacks against the undead.
Those venturing into Skyrim's deepest underground reaches should be wary of chaurus - giant insects that spit poison and bite with razor-sharp mandibles.
Elytra are mantis-like arthropods indigenous to the Shivering Isles. Those from the Mania region are more colorful than, but otherwise identical to, their counterparts from Dementia.
Frost giants are elusive and rarely seen in Tamriel. Their icy blue blood carries regenerative properties, which are hindered by fire.
When stationary, gargoyles form a stony skin to disguise themselves as statues, bursting forth to ambush the unsuspecting with deadly claws that drain their victims' life forces.
Giants are semi-nomadic, migrating with their mammoth herds to establish camps across Skyrim. They are generally peaceful, so long as potential threats keep their distance.
Wanderers should steer clear of the camps of giants, lest they find themselves the target of powerful blows from the giants' clubs... or the wrath of their mammoths.
Goblins are a rare sight in Skyrim, found along its borders with Hammerfell and Morrowind. They share a similar stature with rieklings, their distant cousins.
Some scholars insist that goblins, despite their proclivity for violence, are less primitive than they seem and are capable of living peacefully with other races.
Few creatures match the cunning, depravity, and repulsiveness of hagravens. A terrible conjoining of woman and bird, they will take through savagery what they cannot win through guile.

The wintry reaches of northern Skyrim are haunted by elemental spirits known as ice wraiths. Their icy glow makes them difficult to see or hit, leaping from the snow as if conjured from the frost itself.
Little is known of the mysterious spriggans, save that they revere Skyrim's forests and will defend these regions with their lives.
Trolls are formidable creatures that can regenerate their health - an ability that fire can all too easily burn away.
Frost trolls are the most fearsome of their kind, aptly named for inhabiting the coldest stretches of the continent.
Though mostly reclusive, trolls can be found in almost any region of Skyrim, both dwelling in the deep underground and wandering the wilderness.

The unicorn is a mythical creature so rare its existence is constantly doubted. Native to the Hunting Grounds, it was conceived by Hircine to be agile and fierce, embodying the qualities of the perfect prey to be hunted.
Vampires are immune to age, resilient to harm, and dependent only upon blood and darkness. As their endless time marches on, they only tend to grow in strength.
Victims of the disease Sanguinare Vampiris will feel suddenly weak during the day and acquire a peculiar thirst, which progresses to Vampirism if not cured within three days.
Vampire Lords can assume a bat-like form at will, complete with deadly talons and leathery wings. While transformed, they wield powerful spells and evade danger by shifting into a cloud of bats.
Only those strong enough to withstand the power bestowed by a Vampire Lord can become one themselves... or otherwise be killed in the process.
While vampires possess unnatural speed, strength, and magical talent, their ability to spread the disease to others - a fate described as worse than death - is among the most frightening.
Vampirism owes its creation to the Daedric Prince Molag Bal, from whom pure-blooded vampires were given their "gift" directly.
"I told him about the most powerful tribe of vampires in Skyrim, the Volkihar, paranoid and cruel, whose very breath could freeze their victims' blood in the veins." - Anonymous, Immortal Blood
There are those who believe that when night descends upon Skyrim, werewolves descend upon the unwary...
Werewolves are skin-changers infected with lycanthropy, a contagious supernatural disease that seeps into the spirit. Their bloodthirsty nature has left them widely reviled.
Lycanthropy was created by the Daedric Prince Hircine, who is known to bestow it upon those he favors. Thus, it is referred to as "Hircine's Gift" - or "Curse," by those who view it as such.
The strength of a werewolf's bloodlust seems to vary, with some maintaining control during a transformation and others becoming little more than feral beasts.
Those with the blood of a werewolf are said to be cursed with wild dreams, seldom benefiting from a restful night's sleep - no matter how comfortable their bed might be.
The true nature of wispmothers, who reside in Skyrim's frozen and mountainous regions, is a mystery. Some believe they are the ghosts of the long-dead Snow Elves.
Wisps may enchant the hapless adventurer, but these ethereal floating entities are usually accompanied by a wispmother, who does not respond kindly to threats against her "children."
The term "daedra" refers to entities that inhabit the planes of Oblivion. Because they are not bound to Nirn, they cannot be permanently killed, only banished.
Recognized by their large head crest, sharp beak, and long talons, clannfears are reptilian daedra that serve many Daedric Princes.
Commonly associated with Molag Bal, daedroths are crocodile-headed daedra that possess long clawed arms, a powerful bite, and a maw that spews flame.
Hungers are vicious daedra that serve Boethiah, using their paralyzing touch, razor-sharp claws, and long tongues to siphon the life from their prey.
Hailing from the murky waters of Apocrypha, lurkers are amphibious daedra that serve their Prince by guarding forbidden knowledge.
Lesser daedra called scamps regularly enter the mortal plane to cause mischief and carry out errands for their Princes - mainly Mehrunes Dagon.
Dremora are a warlike daedric race commonly encountered throughout Oblivion. Highly intelligent, they consider themselves both superior to other daedra and beyond notions of good or evil.
Dremora who serve Daedric Princes exist to fulfill their Princes' purposes and often act as intermediaries for mortals seeking to make pacts with them.
Though mainly followers of Mehrunes Dagon, Dremora are also known to serve other Princes, such as Molag Bal and Boethiah.
The daedra known to themselves as "Kyn" use the term "Dremora" when dealing with mortals to prevent their true names from being weaponized against them.
Dremora society is a tiered clan system that values oaths, pride, and loyalty - to both the clan and to the lord they serve, whom they also venerate as a god.
Dremora are fierce combatants not only due to their prowess as warriors and sorcerers, but also because, as creatures of Oblivion, they face no fear of death.
Golden Saints are proud daedric warriors tasked with guarding the Mania half of the Shivering Isles. They are the rivals of the Dark Seducers, with whom they compete eternally for Sheogorath's favor.
In spite of their kind name and appearance, the Golden Saints are an arrogant race with little love for mortals, quick to anger and cruel in their punishments.
The Golden Saints and Dark Seducers refer to themselves as "the Aureal" and "the Mazken," respectively, and both treat all men as inferior.

Dark Seducers are cunning daedric warriors tasked with guarding the Dementia half of the Shivering Isles. They are the rivals of the Golden Saints, with whom they compete eternally for Sheogorath's favor.
Despite their menacing name and appearance, the Dark Seducers are an outwardly polite race with more patience for mortals than their rivals... to an extent.

"Any resident of the Shivering Isles can confirm that it is unwise to provoke the Golden Saints and Dark Seducers. They thrive on conflict and warfare, and are quick to punish any and all who disobey." - Andoche Marie, Saints and Seducers
Daedric Princes are god-like beings that inhabit the realms of Oblivion. Considered evil by most, their worshippers must build shrines to them far from civilized places.
Daedric Princes are the most powerful of the daedra and thus worshipped by some mortals as deities. Each oversees their own plane of Oblivion and may manifest in male or female forms.
Azura is the Daedric Prince of dusk and dawn - the magic between realms of twilight. She is one of the few of her kind not considered by mortals to be wholly evil.
Boethiah is the Daedric Prince of deceit, conspiracy, and secret plots of murder. She is revered in Morrowind, where many Dark Elves regard her as their god-ancestor.
Clavicus Vile is the Daedric Prince of power, trickery, and bargains, often accompanied by his hound, Barbas. He enjoys enticing mortals with tempting pacts that they usually come to regret.
Hermaeus Mora is the Daedric Prince of fate, knowledge, and memory. In his rare dealings with mortals, he usually chooses to appear as a grotesque mass of tentacles.
Hircine is the Daedric Prince of the hunt and master of beasts. He acts as the guardian of were-creatures, commonly referred to as his "children."
Jyggalag is the Daedric Prince of logical order and deduction. He was cursed in antiquity to live as Sheogorath, resuming his true form to reclaim the Shivering Isles at the end of every era.
Malacath is the Daedric Prince of curses and the spurned, venerated by the Orcs. Legend suggests he was once an Aedra who was transformed by Boethiah into his current, vengeful form.
Mehrunes Dagon is the Daedric Prince of destruction, revolution, and ambition. He caused the Oblivion Crisis when he attempted to enter Tamriel in his true and terrible form.
Mephala is the Daedric Prince of lies, sex, and secrets, ever weaving webs of intrigue and terror. She thoroughly enjoys meddling in the affairs of mortals.
Meridia is the Daedric Prince of life and light who despises undead in any form. She has a reputation for benevolence, but treats mortals as mere assets.
Molag Bal is the Daedric Prince of brutality and enslavement. His ultimate desire is to reap the souls of all mortals by sowing strife and discord in the mortal realms.
Namira is the Daedric Prince of darkness and revulsion. As the patron of squalor and vermin, she holds ties to disease, insects, and other repulsive creatures.
Nocturnal is the Daedric Prince of night and mystery, associated with ravens and crows. Many thieves take her as their patron, striving to become one with the shadows she commands.
Peryite is the Daedric Prince of tasks, natural order, and pestilence. Despite being portrayed as a dragon, he is considered one of the weakest of his kind.
Sanguine is the Daedric Prince of debauchery and dark indulgence. He is known for hosting lavish parties where the revelry is always mixed with malice.
Sheogorath is the Daedric Prince of madness and creativity. He is utterly unpredictable and may hinder or help any mortal unlucky enough to cross his path.
Vaermina is the Daedric Prince of dreams, nightmares, and evil omens. There was once a temple near Dawnstar dedicated to her worship.
The religion of the Eight Divines is a fusion of the Aldmeri and Nordic pantheons instituted by Saint Alessia in the First Era. Talos was declared the ninth Divine in the early Third Era.
Akatosh, the dragon god of time, is the chief deity of the Divines and defender of the Empire, upholding the qualities of endurance, invincibility, and everlasting legitimacy.
The deities of the Nordic pantheon are divided into several groups: the Dead Gods, the Hearth Gods, the Twilight God (Alduin), and the Testing Gods such as Orkey, who is depicted as a serpent.
The Aedra of the Imperial Pantheon are viewed as benevolent beings for sacrificing their own energy to imbue the world with life and natural laws.

"I begin every service in the temple with a prayer to praise Alduin (oh great god of time!), followed by a prayer to keep him at bay (may your slumber stretch on for a thousand generations!)." - High Priest Ingurt, Divines and the Nords
Kynareth, called Kyne by the Nords, is the goddess of the Storm and widowed warrior-wife of Shor. She guides fallen souls to Sovngarde, earning her the moniker "Kiss at the End."
Mara is the mother-goddess of fertility and compassion. The Nords regard her as a handmaiden of Kyne and concubine of Shor - the Nordic aspect of Lorkhan.
Talos, the hero-god of mankind, was a mortal and Dragonborn named Tiber Septim who ascended to godhood upon his death. His worship was banned in the Fourth Era as part of the White-Gold Concordat.
Shrines in the temples of Skyrim can heal the sick and confer divine blessings. As one god's blessing replaces another, their benefits cannot be hoarded.
Ysmir, the "Dragon of the North," is an important hero-god of the Nords and a title bestowed upon great heroes such as Tiber Septim, with King Wulfharth as the first.
No credible stories explain how dragons came to be. They are said to have simply always been - eternal and unchanging, neither born nor hatched, yet given to feelings of pride and melancholy.
Though they may seem beast-like, dragons are immortal and highly intelligent, once revered as gods by the ancient Nords.
When dragons breathe magic, such as flames or frost, they invoke the power of their ancient language. A battle between two dragons is, in fact, a deadly verbal debate.
"Dragons, being dragons, embraced their role as god-kings over men... Were they not superior in every way to the hordes of small, soft creatures that worshipped them?" - Torhal Bjorik, The Dragon War
Once, the dragons sought to eliminate or enslave all mortal races. Given the chance, they would surely do so again...
Until now, most citizens of Tamriel believed dragons to be nothing more than myth. Their sudden return is a source of both awe and terror.

Stripped of their power in the Dragon War, dragons were largely killed off thereafter and vanished from Tamriel. The few who survived did so in seclusion and obscurity, believed extinct by almost all.
Nordic myth regards Alduin as a harbinger of the apocalypse who is older than Nirn itself, having destroyed the last world to create the current one.
Alduin is the self-proclaimed First-Born of Akatosh who, during the days of the Dragon Cult, forsook his destiny as the World-Eater to conquer Mundus for himself.

"And the Scrolls have foretold, of black wings in the cold, That when brothers wage war come unfurled! Alduin, Bane of Kings, ancient shadow unbound, With a hunger to swallow the world!" - Song of the Dragonborn
Not much is known about Odahviing's life before his burial, but he is assumed to have served Alduin as a soldier during the Dragon War, in which he was likely slain.
Originally the first lieutenant and brother of Alduin, Paarthurnax betrayed his kin and taught the power of the Voice to mankind, thereby creating the first Tongues.
"Maw unleashing razor snow, Of dragons from the blue brought down, Births the walking winter's woe, The High King in his Jagged Crown." - Ancient Nord Verse
As the immortal children of Akatosh, dragons are uniquely attuned to the flow of time and feel an innate urge to dominate others that is near-impossible to overcome.
The link between a dragon's soul and its remains is stronger than that of a mortal, allowing it to rise again after defeat. Only when absorbed by another dov can it be permanently destroyed.
Although some tales of old recount dragons coming to Tamriel from Atmora, most agree that they originate from the continent of Akavir, meaning "Dragon Land."
While dragons, and Dragonborn, possess an innate understanding of the Dragon Language - properly known as Thu'um - anyone can learn to shout with adequate training.
Despite supposedly existing before time was a concept, some dragons are described as more ancient than others and are therefore not all equal in power.
While all dragons are fearsome, some are more powerful than others, with their might reflected by their hue. Beyond this, each dragon bears its own unique head shape, horns, and other attributes.
Frost dragons are larger than their weaker brethren and harness the power of their namesake to deliver devastating breath attacks that drain their targets' stamina.
Revered dragons stand out from their kin with a beaked mouth and distinct lack of teeth. The true danger lies in their unique shout, which drains the life force of its unlucky targets.
Found only on Solstheim, serpentine dragons are also unique for their lack of scutes and oversized lower jaws, which give them a distinctive underbite.
For all of Skyrim's beauty, her dangers are plentiful. Brave explorers will face all manner of enemies on their journeys, from restless spirits and vampires to otherworldly monsters.
Restless dead still haunt Ayleid ruins, long after their kind was overthrown and then faded from Tamriel. The deadliest of these are formidable sorcerer liches.
Even the most foolhardy adventurers must be cautious of bandits, who lead lives of plunder in Skyrim's less populated regions.
In life, the Dragon Priests ruled over men with the power of kings in service to their dragon gods - alas for those who dare disturb their ages-long slumber.

No one is certain why the draugr still walk the halls of their burial crypts, but some believe they served the dragons and their priests ages ago... and have been cursed with undeath for their treachery.
Woe to the unwary explorer who delves deep into the burial crypts of the ancient Nords and disturbs the draugr that dwell within.
Draugr vary greatly in strength and skill - perhaps matching their battle prowess prior to undeath - with the more formidable among them wielding more impressive equipment.
Centuries of rot have undone even the best embalming techniques of the ancient Nords, slowly giving way to the draugr's present grotesque forms.
The long-vanished Dwemer built many automatons that continue to function to this day, thanks to the advanced magic and technology of their construction.
Dwarven animunculi tirelessly patrol the ruins of their time-lost masters, regarding any who venture within as trespassers to be attacked on sight.
Of all the automatons left behind by the Dwemer, Dwarven Centurions are among the most technologically impressive - and deadly. They guard Dwemer ruins as if their masters still walked the halls.
What the Dwarven Sphere lacks in strength, it makes up for in agility, attacking any foe who wanders too close with lunging strikes or bolts from its arm-mounted crossbow.
Arachnid-shaped automatons known as Dwarven spiders are a common sight in Dwarven ruins. Although not built for combat, they are agile and use their many legs to stab intruders.
The Falmer are twisted creatures that dwell in Skyrim's deepest reaches. They have but one desire: to destroy the surface world and all who dwell above.
Falmer tend to make their lairs near Dwemer technology, as if unwilling to wander far from where their ancestors took shelter from the Nords.
Scholars assume that the Falmer were rendered blind by generations of living underground; over time, their other senses became more acute as a result.
Long thought extinct at the hands of the Nords, the Falmer are actually the disfigured remnants of the Snow Elves, twisted by centuries of subterranean slavery under the Dwemer.
The Forsworn have long claimed to be the true owners of the Reach and have only begrudgingly accepted Nord rule over the centuries.
Cultists are enigmatic followers of Miraak who reside in his temple on Solstheim and carry out his wishes, whatever they may be.
Bone colossi are large undead constructs made from assorted bones that can be summoned by powerful necromancers.
The restless dead sometimes manifest as ghosts to exact their revenge upon the living. These disembodied souls are resistant to blows from non-magical weaponry.
When souls trapped in black soul gems are used to power an enchantment, their remnants are sent to the Soul Cairn to wander for eternity.
Liches are necromancers who have shed mortality itself to embrace the most sophisticated form of undeath. Dragon Priests are a particular Nordic variety.
In some of Skyrim's darkest recesses, where the living fear to tread, the bones of the dead still walk. These skeletons feel no pain or remorse... and deserve no mercy.
Skeletons are a type of reanimated undead, often raised by necromancers, that are quicker and sturdier than zombies.
Zombies are undead humanoids that sometimes roam in hordes, carry basic weapons, and are mostly vulnerable to fire.
Redguard mercenaries from Hammerfell have recently been spotted in Skyrim. They claim to be searching for a fugitive, but remain secretive about their true motives.
The Blades Guard defended the Septim emperors for centuries as knights and spies. Sworn to serve the Dragonborn, they hold Talos as their patron deity.
The Blades formed from a splinter faction of the Akaviri Dragonguard, which disbanded in disgrace following the assassination of Emperor Reman III at the end of the First Era.
Formally disbanded after the Great War and ruthlessly hunted by the Thalmor, the Blades' remaining members have gone into hiding to await the return of a worthy Dragonborn.
With the Septim Dynasty sundered, the Blades no longer answer to the Empire. They have reformed following Alduin's return to assume the dragonslaying legacy of their forebears.
Operating in strict secrecy, the Blades shared their missions with only an elite few and maintained hidden strongholds across Tamriel where they could live and train unseen.
The Greybeards are an honored cult of monks who live at the ancient monastery of High Hrothgar. They are the most famous of the Tongues, or masters of the Voice.
The Greybeards have long mistrusted and feared the Blades, viewing them as violent Akaviri barbarians bent on turning the Dragonborn away from the path of wisdom.
Followers of the Way of the Voice are generally peaceful, tolerating violence only in times of "true need."
Moth Priests are members of the Cult of the Ancestor Moth who believe their sacred duty is to study the Elder Scrolls - an act that often renders them blind.
The Mythic Dawn was a cult that believed Tamriel was Lorkhan's realm, seized by the Aedra through betrayal. They called upon Mehrunes Dagon to liberate it by waging the Oblivion Crisis.
The Mythic Dawn called their enemies the "Dragon's Blood," evoking Queen Alessia's covenant with Akatosh that shielded Nirn from Oblivion - and the line of rulers who kept the Dragonfires burning.
The primary task of the Penitus Oculatus (meaning "the Inner Eyes") is to protect the Emperor, serving as the eyes, sword, and shield of the Mede Dynasty.
The Penitus Oculatus demands its agents always be ready to kill, employing a brutal recruitment process to root out the squeamish and weak-willed.
The Thalmor are the governing council of the Third Aldmeri Dominion. They maintain an embassy in Skyrim and are known to capture and imprison anyone who questions their doctrines.
The First Aldmeri Dominion was an empire founded by Queen Ayrenn in 2E 580. Each of its three incarnations has sought the same objective: to reassert Elven dominance over Tamriel.
The Vigil of Stendarr is an order of holy warriors who dedicate themselves to eradicating daedra and other "abominations" in the name of the Divine they revere.
Bards can be heard playing and singing a variety of songs in taverns throughout Skyrim - sometimes at the request of patrons.
Adventurers need not face the perils of their journeys alone. Many across the realm seek companions in the trials and triumphs of their quests, drawn together by common goals.
Breaking the law is frowned upon by most people. Those with a penchant for crime will quickly overstay their welcome among decent folk.
Crimes earn bounties in the holds where they occur - if someone happens to witness them. Local guards will attempt an arrest, and fleeing only invites a chase.
Hoarding more loot than can be easily carried often proves unwise. An overburdened traveler will find their journey slowed and threats harder to evade.
Rumor has it that the sewers of Riften are home to a sculptor who works in the medium of flesh, able to alter faces beyond recognition.
Farmers tend to their land in rural areas outside of larger cities, sometimes seeking extra hands to help with their labors.
"The Empire is Law. The Law is Sacred." - Imperial Septim inscription
The High King or Queen of Skyrim inherits the throne by birth and holds it for life. When no clear heir exists, a successor is chosen by a Moot of jarls.
Housecarls are personal bodyguards appointed to jarls and their thanes, sworn to protect them with their very lives.
Game is abundant in Skyrim's countryside, ripe for the harvest. Many hunters roam the wilds in pursuit of elk and other animals, occasionally trading their spoils along the way.
Each of Skyrim's nine holds is governed by a jarl. They are largely autonomous, yet they all swear fealty to the High King or Queen.
Caravans of Khajiit merchants travel across Skyrim, selling rare curios and items from other provinces. Their reputation for trading in illegal substances has led cities to forbid them entry.
Most merchants open their shops a few hours after dawn and close just after sunset. If a shop is closed, return in the morning... or pick the lock to browse for free.
Merchants offer a variety of goods for sale and may buy unwanted items at fair prices. Those skilled in persuasion can try bartering for more favorable deals.
Nirn is orbited by two moons: Masser, the larger of the two, and Secunda. Nordic myth relates them to a pair of twins who became lost inside a magical blizzard.
A map is just one way to navigate Skyrim. Road signs are posted at crossroads throughout the province, pointing travelers toward cities, villages, and prominent landmarks.
Oblivion Gates are otherworldly portals used by daedric forces to travel between their various realms and Mundus.
The sale and furnishing of houses are left to a jarl's steward. Several properties are available for purchase in Skyrim's major cities.
A bounty can be paid off or resolved by serving time in jail. Once imprisoned, an escape can always be attempted...
Not all coin is honest, and not all work is clean. Those willing to get their hands dirty may find good pay either way.
Books are valuable resources for gaining knowledge, learning spells or skills, and catching a glimpse into the storied past.
The ports of Skyrim are filled with seaworthy ships, whereas the icy depths of the Sea of Ghosts are strewn with the wreckage of less fortunate sailors.
Throughout the wilderness stand runed stones attuned to the heavens. Although their origins are a mystery, they are reputed to grant power to those deemed worthy.
The standing stones that dot Skyrim's landscape correspond to the constellations within Tamriel's night sky. Among them, the Warrior, the Mage, and the Thief stand together as the "guardians."
Preferably done without detection or bloodshed, stealing is one of the easiest ways to acquire gold... or become a wanted criminal.
Skyrim's harsh wilderness and unrelenting cold may pose great challenges to the ill-prepared. Only the hardiest explorers can survive her treacherous beauty and stave off hunger and fatigue.
Thane is an honorary title granted by the jarl of a hold to individuals of high esteem, oftentimes in recognition of heroic deeds.
"Whatever lay beyond the door, she thought, must be of sufficient value to merit such protection." - Aniis Noru, Surfeit of Thieves
Many of Skyrim's bards are graduates of the Bards College in Solitude, a musical school that teaches tale-telling and song.
The Bards College is Skyrim's foremost school for aspiring bards - or "skalds," as they are known in the province.
It is said that prospective members of the Dark Brotherhood must be contacted directly, indicating just how selective the shadowy assassins are in their recruitment.
A Dark Brotherhood assassin practices the art of murder, understanding that every kill demands payment - in the form of gold, a jail cell, or more bloodshed.
The Dark Brotherhood is but a shadow of its former self. Once a feared cult of assassins devoted to the Night Mother, it now operates as little more than a band of murderers for hire.
The ruling council of the Dark Brotherhood, called the Black Hand, consists of four Speakers and one Listener, symbolizing four fingers and a thumb.
When a person prays for the death of another, the Night Mother hears and relays the details to her Listener. She is believed to be voicing the will of Sithis.
"Sweet Mother, sweet Mother, send your child unto me, for the sins of the unworthy must be baptized in blood and fear." - Black Sacrament chant
The Sanctuary hidden in the pine forest near Falkreath is believed to be the last remaining refuge of the Dark Brotherhood in all of Tamriel.
Long associated with the Dark Brotherhood, the mysterious black horse named Shadowmere will rise again within days of its supposed demise - if an enemy somehow manages to slay the resilient steed.
The Shadowscales were a long-standing order of Argonian assassins born under the sign of the Shadow, offered to the Dark Brotherhood at birth for training in stealth and assassination.
As gruesome as the Black Sacrament ritual may be, more disturbing is its intention: the summoning of a mysterious assassin to kill an unsuspecting victim in exchange for gold.
Most of the city of Winterhold was lost to the sea in the Great Collapse of 4E 122, but the College was left mysteriously unharmed.
The College of Winterhold is a school of magic where aspiring mages who prove their skill may study the arcane arts.
The secretive nature of the College of Winterhold's mages has only deepened the local Nords' suspicion of magic, inciting widespread distrust of the institution and its members.
Those granted admission to the College of Winterhold may further their studies in the arcane by attending lectures, held daily within the Hall of the Elements.
While the mages of the College of Winterhold share knowledge freely amongst themselves, they do not typically offer their services to outsiders.

The Arcaneum of the College of Winterhold contains a wealth of knowledge amassed over the course of centuries, accessible to those who require it, but kept under the ever-watchful eye of its librarian.
Warriors seeking adventure and kinship may join the Companions in Whiterun, a guild that traces its legacy back to the original Five Hundred Companions of Ysgramor.
The Circle of Jorrvaskr comprises the most trusted veterans among the ranks of the Companions. They venerate the old ways of "honor through blood" and secretly practice lycanthropy.
The Companions' only recognized leader is the Harbinger, named after Ysgramor, the "harbinger of us all." Their word is highly respected both within Jorrvaskr and around all the nine holds.
According to local legend, the time-honored mead hall of Jorrvaskr is the oldest building in Whiterun. It provides sanctuary to the warriors' guild of the Companions.
Though its influence has dwindled in recent years, the presence of the Thieves Guild beneath the streets of Riften has earned the city a rather unsavory reputation.
The Thieves Guild has a strong presence in the city of Riften and has been known to recruit those gifted in the art of stealth.
The Thieves Guild maintains power in politics and law enforcement through the bribery, intimidation, and extortion of officials.
Fences are discreet merchants who will purchase stolen items, erasing all evidence of theft. Members of the Thieves Guild are offered this service upon joining.
Although violence is more tolerated within Skyrim's branch, members of the Thieves Guild are generally bound not to rob each other, target the poor, or kill anyone while thieving.
Shadowmarks work as a secret language among thieves, etched onto buildings to guide one another through the dangers of their trade and toward coveted treasures.
Like any trade guild, the Thieves Guild is an organization of professionals - except that, in this case, its members specialize in burglary, pickpocketing, and other illicit activities.
Authorities have historically turned a blind eye to the Thieves Guild, as long as it maintained order in the underworld and kept its members in check.
The hardships of life in Skyrim leave little room for lengthy courtship. Many seeking marriage simply wear an Amulet of Mara to signal their interest.
Bonemold, as the name suggests, is a heavy crafting material made from bone reinforced with resin, commonly molded into armor in Morrowind.
Chitin is a type of light armor from Morrowind that is crafted from insect shells layered together with resinous glues.
Among the rarest and most coveted gear is that of daedric craft, wielded by the forces of Oblivion. Forged from ebony and infused with a daedra's essence, it requires the skill of a master smith.
Ebony is a durable volcanic glass refined by folding many times upon itself. Said to be the crystallized blood of Lorkhan, it is one of Tamriel's most precious substances.
Elven weapons and armor are lightweight and ornately designed, forged from moonstone through techniques perfected by the High Elves.
Glass weapons and armor, crafted from a rare volcanic crystal called malachite, are highly sought after for their durability and lightness.
Iron may be a commonplace material, but it is battle-tried and true, often used in crafting for its durability and abundance.
A mage's robes trade the protection of armor for greater freedom of spellcasting. They often carry enchantments to enhance the wearer's magical abilities.

The devices left behind by the Dwemer mystify adventurers and scholars alike. Some are repositories of forgotten knowledge, while others reveal hidden chambers in the long-empty halls of their makers.
Ingredients can be harvested from plants and slain creatures or purchased from vendors, and each possesses unique magical and alchemical potential.
Soul gems are sized according to the strength of souls they can capture, ranging from petty to grand. Molag Bal is rumored to have created them with a portion of his infernal power.
Artifacts are items of significant power or fame. Some even seem to have a will of their own, never staying with one owner for long.
Every daedric artifact carries the essence of a Daedric Prince within. Mortals who wield them spread that Prince's reach a little further across the realms.
Dawnfang and Duskfang are forms taken by an evidently sentient blood-drinker longsword, whose shapeshifting ability and serpent-like appearance are reminiscent of the Tsaesci who forged it.

The Elder Scrolls are occasionally used to divine prophecies, be it only a portion of their power. All reflections witnessed within the Scrolls are true - especially the falsehoods - which drives many who read them to madness.
Legend holds that the highest-ranking Dragon Priests were granted magical masks - strange artifacts that defy the laws of time and grant their wearers powerful enchantments.
While adventuring, it is possible to come across maps that indicate the whereabouts of hidden treasures. Deciphering their clues takes a keen mind, familiar with Skyrim's less-traveled reaches.
War axes strike a balance between speed and power, swinging faster than maces, and delivering more damage than swords.
Two-handed weapons deal more damage with greater reach than their one-handed counterparts. They are slower to wield, however, and poorly timed attacks can be easily evaded or countered.
Crossbows are slow to reload, but their bolts strike with a force few bows can match. They can be held at the ready without strain, lending the marksman more time to aim true.
The short blade and hilt of a dagger allow for swift strikes in close quarters, making it a well-suited weapon for the nimble and stealthy.
The power of enchanted weapons may fade with use, but can be replenished at the expense of filled soul gems.
Poison coated on a blade will wear off between strikes and must be reapplied to maintain its potency.
Depending on their length and balance, swords are typically lighter and more agile to wield than axes or maces.
Warhammers are slow and cumbersome, demanding two strong hands to wield them, but their power is devastating - a well-placed blow can stagger even the largest foes.
The bold adventurer may unearth hidden treasures in Skyrim's darkest depths, but countless dangers await in the shadows... and some are better left undisturbed.
Dragons tend to make their lairs atop secluded mountain peaks or near Nordic ruins. They seem to guard - or are perhaps simply drawn to - word walls etched with the Dragon Language.
The wilds of Skyrim are scattered with large burial mounds, said to entomb the remains of ancient dragons that fell in the Dragon War - a tale once thought to be mere legend...
Eastmarch lies along Skyrim's eastern border with Morrowind. Dominated by expansive hot springs, it is mostly rural apart from its capital, Windhelm.
Falkreath Hold is well known for its dense pine forests and age-old connection to death, since its namesake capital features the largest graveyard in Skyrim.
Haafingar is a coastal hold in northwestern Skyrim featuring the famed city of Solitude. It borders High Rock to the west, where the Druadach Mountains begin to diminish.
Dry ground can be difficult to find in the hold of Hjaalmarch, where eerie marshlands prevail. Its capital, Morthal, is said to be named after the legendary hero Morihaus.
The Pale was named for the hold's white tundra and the fair skin of the local Nords. Its capital, Dawnstar, is one of the busiest ports in Skyrim.
The Reach is a mountainous hold in southwestern Skyrim adjacent to High Rock and Hammerfell. Markarth, its capital, was once a stronghold of the Dwemer.
In southeastern Skyrim lies the Rift, a hold noted for its mild climate and autumnal forests. Riften, its capital, once hosted a vast trading network with Morrowind.
At the heart of Skyrim lies Whiterun Hold, with flat tundra plains and the Throat of the World. Its namesake capital sits amid fertile farmlands that feed much of the province.
The northernmost reaches of Skyrim belong to Winterhold, marked by harsh and snow-blown landscapes. Most of its residents are fisherfolk who work on the Sea of Ghosts.
Deposits of precious ores can be found in the underground throughout Skyrim, with many of the most prosperous sites actively mined.
Apocrypha is the realm of Hermaeus Mora, an endless library stacked from root to sky with forbidden knowledge. Many mortal minds have fallen to madness under the burden of its secrets.
Upon death, a vampire's soul is sent to Coldharbor, the dreadful realm of Molag Bal - a fate shared by mortals who make dealings with this Daedric Prince.
Mehrunes Dagon's realm is known as the Deadlands, rife with the destructive forces of change. It is carved by lakes of molten fire that are strewn with scorched islands and ruined structures.
Evergloam is Nocturnal's ever-shifting domain of twilight and gloom that seems somehow adjacent to all other planes of reality. It can almost be glimpsed in the dark with a quick turn and glance.
Hircine's domain is an endless forest where the Lord of the Hunt and his huntsmen pursue great beasts, people, and even their own kind in a never-ending cycle of violence and rebirth.
The Shivering Isles, ruled by Sheogorath, are divided into two parts: Mania in the north and Dementia in the south, mirroring the mad god's own split personality.
There are planes of Oblivion unruled by any Daedric Prince. The Soul Cairn is one such place... though it is not without masters of its own.
Taverns are establishments found throughout Skyrim that offer a respite from the elements, as well as the company of locals to mingle with.
Innkeepers overhear many rumors and may provide valuable insights to the eager explorer, as well as food for trade.
Many inns offer lodgings for rent, granting the weary adventurer a restful night away from home. A proper bed usually allows for better sleep than a bedroll laid out in the cold.
Beneath Skyrim lies the legendary Blackreach: a long-forgotten realm of time-worn Dwarven ruins and monsters too horrible to venture into the light above.
Blackreach is an immense, naturally-lit cavern that can be accessed through certain Dwarven ruins and once served as a highway connecting several Dwemeri cities.
The highest mountain in all of Tamriel is Skyrim's Throat of the World. The reclusive Greybeards reside near the summit, in the windswept halls of High Hrothgar.

The labyrinth for which Labyrinthian is known was built by Archmage Shalidor in the First Era. The ruins themselves are much older, being what remains of the city of Bromjunaar, capital of the Dragon Cult.
Lake Ilinalta is the largest lake in Skyrim and the source of the White River. Local legend claims it is cursed on account of its tendency to swallow missing travelers.

Deep within the Velothi Mountains stands Skuldafn, an ancient Nord temple that holds the only known portal into Sovngarde. Through it, mortals may walk among the dead without dying - if they are able to open it.
What remains of the civilization of the Snow Elves lies hidden away in remote mountain passes, spared from Nordic conquest by their seclusion.
The Chantry of Auri-El was at last overwhelmed by the sheer numbers of the Falmer sometime in the First Era, and so fell the final bastion of the Snow Elves.

The Amulet of Kings symbolized the divine right of the Cyrodiilic emperors. Its near four-thousand-year history ended when it was shattered in the Third Era to seal shut the gates of Oblivion forever.
Barenziah was a long-lived Dunmer woman who became the first Queen of Morrowind in the Third Era, serving as a vassal ruler to the Emperor of Tamriel.
Dagoth Ur wreaked havoc on Morrowind for centuries, drawing power from the depths of Red Mountain to make himself nearly invincible. He was finally defeated by the Nerevarine in the late Third Era.
Dragon Breaks occur when the flow of time is fractured, historically blamed on mortals meddling in divine matters. They often precede significant changes in Tamriel that strain mortal comprehension.
The Dragon War of the late Merethic Era began when the Nords rebelled against Alduin's great cruelty. After a long and dreadful struggle, they defeated their dragon overlords.
Saint Alessia was long hailed as the first Dragonborn in history, until Miraak's reappearance in the Fourth Era raised a far older claim to the title.
"Good business for the East Empire Company means all the more gold for the Empire." - Common phrase
The Gray Fox is the persona of a mysterious master thief that steals the identity of anyone who dons the cursed Gray Cowl of Nocturnal.
The Great War was a large-scale conflict that occurred in Cyrodiil and Hammerfell between the Third Empire of Tamriel and the invading Aldmeri Dominion from 4E 171 to 4E 175.
Only by signing the peace treaty known as the White-Gold Concordat was the Empire able to survive the onslaught of the high-elven Aldmeri Dominion, and thus end the Great War.
Empress Katariah I was the thirteenth ruler of the Septim Dynasty, presiding over the Third Empire from 3E 153 to 3E 200. The personal ship of Emperor Titus Mede II was named in her honor.

The Nord heroes Felldir the Old, Gormlaith Golden-Hilt, and Hakon One-Eye used the Dragonrend shout and an Elder Scroll to cast Alduin adrift through time - an act that granted mankind the edge to end the Dragon War.

"...When the Dragonborn Ruler loses his throne and the White Tower falls, When the Snow Tower lies sundered, kingless, bleeding, The World-Eater wakes and the Wheel turns upon the Last Dragonborn." - Prophecy of the Dragonborn
Dragonborn, or Dovahkiin in the Dragon Language, are mortals who possess the soul of a dragon. They are believed to appear in the world during times of great need at the behest of the gods.

"Very few realize that being Dragonborn is not a simple matter of heredity - being the blessing of Akatosh Himself, it is beyond our understanding exactly how and why it is bestowed." - Emelene Madrine, The Book of the Dragonborn
The Greybeards follow the teachings of Jurgen Windcaller, who believed that the power of the Voice was a means of attaining enlightenment.
The Staff of Worms was once owned by Mannimarco, the King of Worms, an Altmer lich who founded the Order of the Black Worm.
Miraak is the First Dragonborn and a former Dragon Priest. He rebelled against the dragons as Hermaeus Mora's champion after refusing to help the ancient Nords defeat Alduin.

The Empire withdrew its legions from Morrowind during the Oblivion Crisis, and lacked the strength to return. This seeming indifference to their plight drove the Dunmer to retake their homeland for themselves.

The Oblivion Crisis was a total war between the people of Tamriel and the invading daedric hordes of Mehrunes Dagon. It began with the assassination of Uriel Septim VII and all his known heirs in 3E 433.
Myths passed down by the Reachmen tell of a mighty king who, armed with a flaming sword, rallied his people to repel the armies of Cyrodiil in the First Era.
The "Red Year" was the name given to the disaster of 4E 5 when the meteor Baar Dau crashed into Vivec City, leading to the eruption of Red Mountain.
Saint Jiub the Eradicator is a hero of Morrowind, widely esteemed for driving the cliff racers from the island of Vvardenfell.
The Septim Dynasty ended with the death of Martin Septim in 3E 433, when he sacrificed himself to save the world from the Oblivion Crisis, thereby ushering in the Fourth Era.
Despite being revered as a god by some, Sithis is neither aedric nor daedric in nature; rather, he personifies the primordial state of chaos.

"Skyrim, also known as the Old Kingdom or the Fatherland, was the first region of Tamriel settled by humans: the hardy, brave, warlike Nords, whose descendants still occupy this rugged land." - Pocket Guide to the Empire, 1st Edition/Skyrim

The Soulburst of 2E 578 was a massive arcane explosion caused when Emperor Varen Aquilarios attempted a ritual to become Dragonborn. It sundered the veil between Nirn and Oblivion, unleashing a daedric invasion known as the Planemeld.
Sovngarde is the storied afterlife of the Nords, ruled by Shor as a part of Aetherius. It is where the greatest Nord heroes journey upon death to enjoy an eternity of feasting and revelry.
The Hall of Valor, the legendary mead hall of Sovngarde, may only be entered by those honored Nord dead who triumph in battle against Tsun, Shor's mighty shield-thane.
Sword-singers were Redguard warriors of long ago who followed the "Way of the Sword." They performed astonishing feats of swordsmanship, but today are regarded as little more than myth.
The Mede Dynasty seized the Ruby Throne in 4E 22 with the crowning of the warlord Titus Mede I. Their reign continues with Titus Mede II, the current Emperor of Tamriel.
The War of the Red Diamond began in 3E 121 when Uriel III seized the Imperial throne with his mother, Queen Potema. It ended in 3E 137 with her defeat at the Siege of Solitude.
Atromancy is a branch of Conjuration focused on the summoning of atronachs, elemental daedra from the planes of Oblivion.
"Are you in need of a flame spell? Conjure a Flame Atronach. You'll have command of a dozen such spells in the form of a fiery avatar." - Warlock Aldaale, Where Magical Paths Meet
Regarding combat versatility, battlemages are unmatched. As a fusion of soldier and scholar, they can resolve most conflicts with either spell or sword.
Negative opinions on magic emerged in Skyrim's culture when the Nords blamed mages for the Oblivion Crisis. The old Nordic term for a mage was "clever man."
Spells may be prepared in either hand to be dual-wielded by skilled casters, or held in one hand while the other holds a weapon.
Magicka is the raw energy of magic that flows from Aetherius into Mundus via the sun and stars. Known to mages as the Higher Arts, it has many purposes: to heal, to harm, or to fulfill selfish ends.
Often gathering near ritual or burial sites, Necromancers call upon the dead to fight alongside them in combat.
Necromancy is the practice of manipulating mortal souls and reanimating their corpses. Sometimes called the Dark Arts, it is deemed immoral for disrupting the natural order of life and death.
The School of Alteration focuses on the manipulation of the physical world. It can be used to breathe underwater, harden skin to metal, or create light in darkness.
The School of Conjuration focuses on the summoning of creatures and binding of souls. It can be used to raise the dead, conjure ephemeral weapons, or fill soul gems.
The School of Destruction focuses on the mastery of elemental forces. It can be used to launch ice shards, bathe enemies in flame, or strike them down with lightning.
The School of Illusion focuses on the manipulation of the mind. It can be used to calm or frighten targets, trick the senses, or turn oneself invisible.
The School of Restoration focuses on the mastery over life forces. It can be used to mend wounds, repel the undead, or manifest protective wards.
Scrolls can be purchased from any court wizard in service to a jarl, as well as from certain members of the College of Winterhold.
Armamancy is the practice of conjuring bound weapons. During its brief time in Tamriel, a bound weapon is essentially a daedra confined to a magical form.
Fire is one of the most destructive forces at a mage's disposal, inspiring fear in enemies and burning long after the initial burst of flame.
Mastering Destruction magic requires practice in combat against real foes. To truly understand what it means to kill with fire, the target must be something that screams.
Ice serves as a powerful magical force that not only inflicts harm, but also weakens foes by draining their energy and slowing their movement.
Pacify is a spell from the School of Illusion that compels weaker enemies to cease their attacks for a brief time.
Using Reanimate spells, resourceful mages can compel even corpses to fight for them. Whereas a conjurer is limited to the summons they've learned, fallen enemies are never in short supply.
Shock spells and enchantments inflict damage while draining the target's magicka, making them particularly effective against spellcasters.
By casting Soul Trap on a creature at the moment of its death, a spellcaster may capture its soul in a soul gem - provided one of suitable size is empty and available.
Telekinesis is an Alteration spell that allows the caster to manipulate objects from afar without ever touching them.
Teleportation spells belong to the School of Conjuration, and enable the caster to travel across great distances in an instant.
Wards are protective spells from the school of Restoration that help defend spellcasters from incoming magic and melee attacks.
Staves are powerful tools, but they are merely extensions of their wielders. A mage skilled in Destruction magic will make better use of a fire-spell staff than their peer in Conjuration.
Spell tomes teach the reader a new spell, if they have sufficient skill in the relevant school. They can be purchased from merchants, court wizards, or specialists in the College of Winterhold.
Some of Morrowind's most hostile wilderness is home to the nomadic Dunmeri people known as Ashlanders, who have worshipped the three Good Daedra for millennia.
Ashlanders practice the ancestor-worshipping tribal culture left behind by the House Dunmer. Each tribe is led by the strongest warrior among them, who serves as their Ashkhan.

"The people of Solstheim, the heirs of the Guardian, must remain wary, lest the dark influence of Herma-Mora, or even the Traitor himself, return someday." - Lucius Gallus, The Guardian and the Traitor
Morrowind is governed by the Grand Council of five Great Houses, which function as political parties: House Redoran, House Telvanni, House Sadras, House Indoril, and House Dres.
House Dres is focused mainly on agriculture. Its members, despite their notorious history as slavers, have since accepted Imperial rule and renounced the trade.
House Hlaalu was concerned with business and diplomacy. Its alliance with the Empire, amid rising anti-Imperial sentiment, left it stripped of its Great House status in the early Fourth Era.
House Indoril claims kinship with the Tribunal and boasts such heroes as Indoril Nerevar. Its members are now considered one and the same with the priesthood of the New Temple.
"Duty, gravity, and piety: these are our watchwords. We are the wartime defenders of the House Dunmer of Morrowind." - Vindamea Redoran, Crafting Motif 52
The wizard-lords of House Telvanni have been mostly peaceful throughout history, tending to isolate themselves in mushroom-hut villages to pursue wisdom and arcane mastery.
The Morag Tong is an ancient guild of assassins who serve the Daedric Prince Mephala. The last Emperor of the Reman Dynasty, Reman Cyrodiil III, is counted among their victims.
Sanctioned to perform legal murder, the Morag Tong were frequently hired by the Great Houses to eliminate their rivals - a preferred alternative to open conflict.
Ordinators were guards and priest-soldiers of the Tribunal Temple. Once tasked with enforcing Temple law, they are now persecuted by the New Temple as heretics.
Raven Rock, Solstheim's primary settlement, is firmly under the control of House Redoran, the most powerful of the Great Houses of Morrowind.

Vvardenfell is dominated by a massive volcano called Red Mountain, said to have formed where the Heart of Lorkhan fell. Formerly the tallest mountain in Tamriel, its height was permanently reduced by the Red Year eruption.
The High King of Skyrim formally ceded the island of Solstheim to Morrowind in 4E 16 to serve as a refuge for the Dunmer following the devastation of the Red Year.
Following the disappearance of the Tribunal, the New Temple restored the original Dunmer faith: worship of the three Good Daedra - Azura, Mephala, and Boethiah - referred to as "the Reclamations."
The Tribunal Temple venerated the three "living gods," who exploited Kagrenac's Tools to attain godhood. By the Fourth Era, they were demoted to saints and their worship branded heretical.
Before ascending as the mother-goddess, Almalexia was the mortal wife of Indoril Nerevar. She was worshipped in the Tribunal as the source of compassion and the protector of the weak.
Sotha Sil was the wizard-mystic god and most enigmatic member of the Tribunal, recognized as the patron of artificers and wizards.
Vivec the warrior-poet was the guardian deity of the Tribunal who represented the duality of the Dunmer people with his half-Dunmer, half-Chimer appearance.
The Altmer, also known as High Elves, are the tall elven inhabitants of the Summerset Isles. They are recognized as the longest-living race in Tamriel and the most gifted in the magical arts.
High Elves regard themselves as the purest, most unaltered heirs of the Aldmer - the ancient elves who first arrived on Tamriel from the mythical lost continent of Aldmeris.
The term "high" in "High Elves" is understood to reflect their stature, pride, and cultural elitism. They have long endeavored to found empires on the belief in their own superiority.
The early Aldmer believed they descended from the Aedra (which roughly translates to "our ancestors"), who populated Mundus in the aftermath of Lorkhan's deception.
The Argonians are a reptilian race of beastfolk native to Black Marsh. They excel in stealth and spellcasting, naturally resist poison and disease, and can breathe underwater.

The Hist connects every Argonian in Black Marsh, where its sap is ingested to mark namings, bondings, and passages into death. The darkest rituals use sacrifice to keep lurking things beneath the mires...

Deep within the swamps of Black Marsh grows a race of giant spore trees called the Hist. They are believed to be sentient and to have given life to Argonians, who call themselves "the people of the root."

Centuries of defending their borders have made Argonians masters of guerrilla warfare - fierce enough that, when Oblivion Gates opened in their homeland, the Daedra sealed them shut rather than be overrun.
The Bosmer, also known as Wood Elves, are the elven clanfolk of Valenwood. Well-suited for scouting and thievery, they have an affinity for archery and the ability to command simple-minded beasts.
The Green Pact is a strict code upheld by the Bosmer of Valenwood that forbids harming the forest. Its Meat Mandate involves strict carnivory and the rite of consuming the flesh of fallen foes.
Regarded as the finest archers in Tamriel, Wood Elves can draw and release arrows in one seamless motion - a skill enhanced by their talent for blending into wooded environments.
Wood Elves rejected stiff Aldmeri culture for a simpler existence in harmony with the land. Nimble of body and mind, they are dismissed by their more "civilized" cousins as unruly and naive.
The Bretons are a pale-skinned hybrid race from High Rock, claiming both human and elven ancestry. Their attunement to the mercurial forces of magic distinguishes them from other human races.
Although tales of warring kingdoms account for much of the history of High Rock, the Bretons maintain a rich cultural unity with shared language, bardic traditions, and fabled stories of heroism.
Shorter lifespans put the Bretons at a disadvantage against elves, yet they have produced some of history's greatest mages - second only to the Altmer, with room to surpass them given the chance.
Knighthood is pivotal to the Breton identity, as knights of old liberated their forebears from elven rule and created a legacy for future generations through daring quests for glory.

The Dunmer, also known as Dark Elves, are the gray-skinned elven inhabitants of Morrowind. They possess an innate resistance to fire and can skillfully integrate swords, bows, and Destruction magic in battle.
Outsiders may call the Dunmer proud, clannish, and quick-tempered, yet they value family and loyalty above all. Tempered by centuries of conflict, they remain a resilient and talented people.

The Dark Elves trace their origins to the bygone Chimer, who abandoned the ways of Summerset Isle in pursuit of religious freedom. Guided by the prophet Veloth, they undertook a great exodus to Morrowind.
As punishment for the betrayal of Indoril Nerevar, the Dunmer were cursed by the Daedric Prince Azura with ashen skin and fiery eyes, binding their fate to the Tribunal until the end of time.
The Imperials are the well-spoken human denizens of Cyrodiil, known for the discipline and training of their citizen armies, as well as their respect for the rule of law.

Cosmopolitanism defines Imperial culture, itself a blend of Colovian, Nibenese, and Akaviri traditions. Amid their own divisions and bordering many provinces, the Imperials are practiced at building bridges and keeping order.
Many Imperials still venerate Tiber Septim as a god of the Nine Divines and, knowing well that dynasties rise and fall, hold faith that the Empire will one day reclaim its former glory.
Along with their remarkable skills as light infantry, the Imperials are shrewd diplomats and traders - traits that have enabled them to conquer other nations and establish the Empire.
The Khajiit are a feline race of beastfolk native to Elsweyr. Their intelligence and agility make them natural thieves and acrobats, while their ferocity makes them equally capable warriors.

Khajiit are a type of Betmeri, the so-called "beast races" - a term popularized by the Reman Empire to justify conquering them. Though their nature sometimes draws prejudice, they answer it with pride, not shame.

The Mane is a rare furstock, born when the moons are eclipsed, who serves as the spiritual leader of the Khajiit. Tradition holds that only one can exist at a time, continuously reborn into different bodies.

Nirn's two moons, Masser and Secunda, are venerated as divine in Khajiiti culture. Their phases determine what shape a Khajiit takes at birth, ranging from the diminutive Alfiq to the imposing Pahmar.

The Nords are the tall and fair-haired human denizens of Skyrim, blessed with extraordinary resistance to cold and magical frost. They are renowned as fierce warriors who excel in all manner of warfare.

Ysgramor gathered the Five Hundred Companions to avenge the razing of Saarthal in the Night of Tears. Untold numbers of elves fell to their blades, leaving the Nords with a bitter resentment for elvenkind that endures still.

Some sources trace the lineage of Nords to Atmora, while others believe Kyne breathed life into them atop the Throat of the World. Together, they suggest a migration of their ancestors from Skyrim to Atmora and back.
"Wind is fundamental to Skyrim and the Nords; those that live in the far wastes always carry a wind with them." - Anonymous, Children of the Sky
The Orcs are the mountain-dwelling elves of western Tamriel who founded Orsinium between Hammerfell and Skyrim. Their courage in battle and endurance of hardships mark them as formidable warriors.

The Orsimer revere Malacath as the First Orc and live by his code of honor and vengeance, which includes respect for the forge, a "Blood Price" for crimes, and the belief that death in battle pleases their god.
Not unlike their deity Malacath, the Orcs view themselves as outcasts. They uphold a distinct culture within secluded strongholds, where a single chieftain takes many wives.
Despite their long-standing reputation as mere barbarians, Orcs are as cultured as any other race in Tamriel, having ever striven to be recognized as actual people.
The Redguards are the dark-skinned human denizens of Hammerfell. Their pride and independence of spirit make them better suited as skirmishers or adventurers than as rank-and-file soldiers.
As descendants of the "Warrior Waves," who sailed to Tamriel from the fated land of Yokuda in the First Era, Redguards are renowned for their love of adventure and sailing the high seas.

Nearly all Redguards are taught to fight, but only the fittest become true warriors. They must face death to prove themselves, and it is never far - even their pastime of snake charming tempts its grasp.

The cultural identity of the Redguards is deeply rooted in the sands of the Alik'r Desert. The youth of Hammerfell must undergo a rite of passage in its desolate wastes to prove their endurance and discipline.
The Ayleids were a powerful elven race with a culture steeped in magic and mystery. Having disappeared sometime in the First Era, their age-worn ruins are scattered across Cyrodiil.
Though none have been seen since the Second Era, legend has it that the Ayleids still dwell in the wild reaches of Tamriel.
The Ayleid Empire fell in 1E 243 to the Slave-Queen Alessia, freeing the early Imperials from enslavement with the aid of Pelinal Whitestrake and the Demi-Prince Morihaus.
Dwarven artifacts and ruins are remnants of an ancient race of elves known to historians as the Dwemer, which roughly translates to "Deep Elves."

The dwarves of Tamriel were named by giants and are more properly called the Dwemer. Though relics of their society scatter the continent, the elves themselves vanished millennia ago and are presumed extinct.
Theories vary on why or how the Dwemer disappeared, but some believe that Lord Kagrenac, one of their chief architects, caused the event by tampering with the heart of a god.
The Dragon Cult built high temples to honor the dragons and inter the faithful. Many still stand as forsaken ruins, haunted in undeath by those entombed within.
In days of old, when dragons ruled over the land, there lived mortal men who worshipped them as gods. This Dragon Cult has long since died out, though their ruins still loom over Skyrim.
The ancient Nords followed the Old Ways: the worship of animal gods, most notably the dragon, in the form of totems.
Nordic ruins often contain word walls, inscribed with long-forgotten power through words in the Dragon Language - a series of etched runes resembling claw marks.
The Nords believe the Storm Voice is a gift from Kyne, through which a Tongue can channel their vital essence into a Shout - a powerful form of magic once unique to dragons.
Much like the names of dragons, a shout in the Dragon Language consists of three words of power, with each spoken word increasing the shout's strength.
By invoking Dragon Aspect, skilled wielders of the Voice can enhance their attack power, bolster their defense with spectral armor, and hasten shout recovery.
Shouts may turn the tide of battle when used strategically, but their application extends beyond combat - to swiftly crossing distances, sharpening blades, or altering the weather.
Learning to use the Thu'um typically demands many years of meditation and training. The most powerful Tongues can cause great devastation with so little as a whisper.
The Soul Tear shout binds the soul of its target, siphons their health, and - should they fall within two seconds - raises their corpse to fight for the caster.
The three words of Unrelenting Force (Force, Balance, Push) chain together to hurl objects great distances and briefly render enemies helpless.
The ancient Nords erected many word walls across the land. Their true power lies dormant, awaiting a worthy Dragonborn - and the souls of slain dragons - to awaken it.
Alchemy is the art of mixing, boiling, and distilling raw ingredients to harness their properties for the brewing of potions and poisons.
Alchemists commonly consume samples of ingredients to determine their properties - be they beneficial or harmful.
Poisons are brewed substances that inflict detrimental effects upon their target, capable of damaging health, magicka, and stamina.
The strategic use of potions and other consumables can mean the difference between life and death, granting an upper hand in the midst of battle.
Combat skills must be sharpened with practice, and are best tested when pitted against worthy opponents.
By letting down the bowstring, an archer can reconsider their aim and return an arrow to the quiver. A heavy blade is less forgiving mid-strike.
Precision is vital for an archer faced with a long shot, as they might have only one chance to hit their target before it escapes.
Fully drawing a bow before loosing an arrow results in a more precise and powerful shot with the greatest possible range.
While a weapon in hand might suffice to block incoming blows, a shield provides a more effective means of defense.
Brawls can settle disputes or test an opponent's mettle with nothing but fists. Such contests showcase prowess, and establish respect and camaraderie among friends and rivals alike.
Dual wielding weapons can greatly enhance a combatant's melee damage by allowing both hands to strike simultaneously.
Those trained to use one-handed weapons can adeptly wield daggers, swords, maces, and war axes, leaving their off-hand free to hold a shield or an additional weapon.
Surprise attacks against unsuspecting victims are generally more lethal than ones that are openly declared, even when the same level of force is used.
Those trained to use two-handed weapons deliver deadlier blows with greatswords, battleaxes, and warhammers.
Unarmed combat requires only a fighter's fists, ready even when a blade is out of reach. Some hone this skill deliberately, while the beast races carry claws as weapons all their own.
Understanding the magical properties of enchanted gear requires study at an enchanting table - a process that ultimately results in the items' destruction.
The skills of a smith are used to craft new weapons and armor from raw materials, as well as to improve existing gear.
The efficacy of stealth depends on several factors, such as enemy sightlines, cumbersomeness of worn armor, quickness of pace, and availability of shadow.
The stealthiest approach can still be undone by a single careless footstep, a flickering torch, or the sharp eyes of a watchful guard.
Skills improve through experience and practical application, but may also be taught by those adept in their respective fields.

The Ruby Throne in Cyrodiil's White-Gold Tower has been the ruling seat of the Empire of Tamriel since the First Empire of Saint Alessia. As of the Fourth Era, the Third Empire comprises only Skyrim, High Rock, and Cyrodiil.
Black Marsh, also known as Argonia, is a dense swampland region in southeastern Tamriel inhabited by the Argonians. It is a land teeming with poisonous plants and violent predators.

Cyrodiil, sometimes called "the Heartland," is a temperate province in central Tamriel from which the Imperials hail. It holds the Empire's capital, the Imperial City, with the White-Gold Tower at its heart.
Elsweyr lies on the southern coast of Tamriel and is home to the feline Khajiit. The land is divided by two distinct climates: arid wastes in the north, and fertile jungle in the south.
Hammerfell is a rugged province in western Tamriel from which the Redguards hail. The region boasts a variety of landscapes, including subtropical beaches, lush jungles, and the vast Alik'r Desert.

High Rock in northwestern Tamriel is the homeland of the Bretons and once held the kingdom of the Orcs. Featuring temperate forests, dry badlands, and snowy mountains, it is a land as diverse as its people.

Morrowind is a volcanic region in northeastern Tamriel from which the Dark Elves hail. The mainland is isolated by vast mountain ranges, with the island of Vvardenfell and the ash-spewing Red Mountain at its core.

Skyrim is the northernmost province of Tamriel and homeland of the Nords, who long ago conquered the Snow Elves. It is a cold and rugged region containing four of the five tallest mountains on the continent.
The Summerset Isles lie southwest of Tamriel in the Sea of Pearls and are home to the High Elves. Consisting of fourteen islands, they make up a warm region with colorful forests and idyllic meadows.
Valenwood is a densely forested region in southwestern Tamriel, inhabited by the Wood Elves. Its rainforests are roamed by gigantic, migratory trees whose branches host entire cities.
